item.title: US House to Vote on Bipartisan Bill Protecting Households from Data Center Power Costs
item.description:
US House to Vote on Bipartisan Bill Protecting Households from Data Center Power Costs

The US House of Representatives is expected to vote on the bipartisan ‘Ratepayer Protection Act’ this Wednesday. The legislation aims to prevent the soaring costs associated with data center expansion and power needs from being passed on to average household electricity bills.

🔍 Overview

Introduced by Representative Kathy Castor (D-FL) and Representative Gabe Evans (R-CO), the bill seeks to ensure that large data centers pay their fair share of the costs for expanding the electricity grid. The proposal comes as government officials face pressure to manage the increasing energy demands of the AI industry while protecting consumer affordability and grid reliability.

🧩 How it works

  • Cost Allocation: State utility regulators would be required to consider whether large electricity users should pay for the infrastructure needed to serve them.
  • Capacity Threshold: The proposed rules would require new data centers using at least 20 megawatts to cover the additional power infrastructure costs they create.
  • Rate Reductions: Regulators would have the authority to charge large data centers extra to help lower the bills of other utility customers.
  • State Authority: The bill would give states more freedom to impose conditions, such as requiring data centers to secure new power supplies or placing limits on their electricity usage.

⚙️ Key details

The following reactions and perspectives have been reported regarding the proposed legislation:

Entity or Individual Position Perspective
Hakeem Jeffries House Democratic Leader Called the proposal an ‘appropriate step forward’ but noted ‘more clearly needs to be done.’
Allison Clements Former FERC member Described the bill as a ‘modest step in the right direction’ that signals congressional alignment on protecting customers.
Craig Sundstrom Amazon Energy Policy Director Stated the bill ‘could unlock the investment needed to build new generation and transmission faster.’
Ari Peskoe Harvard Electricity Law Initiative Highlighted that no other industry’s electricity usage has captured so much political attention.
Technology Industry Official (Via Axios) Described certain provisions as an ‘unprecedented level of discriminatory treatment’ for a single industry.

💡 Why it matters

While data centers have existed for decades, the growth of AI has significantly increased the demand for new power plants and grid upgrades. This shift has raised concerns regarding higher costs for households. The bipartisan support for the bill arrives ahead of the November midterm elections, highlighting the political priority of grid reliability and consumer costs. While Amazon suggests the bill could accelerate infrastructure investment, the Data Center Coalition is currently reviewing the legislation. Microsoft, Google, and Nvidia declined to comment, while Meta did not respond to requests for comment.

#DataCenters #EnergyPolicy #ArtificialIntelligence #Legislation

Source: US moves to stop AI data centres from pushing up household electricity bills. Here’s what could change for Americans

item.title: European Energy Sector Updates Cybersecurity Strategies to Address AI-Driven Grid Threats
item.description:
European Energy Sector Updates Cybersecurity Strategies to Address AI-Driven Grid Threats

Experts gathering at the 9th Cybersecurity Forum in Brussels are warning that the European energy sector must close the gap between rapidly evolving cyber threats and practical response capabilities. The forum addresses new risks created by geopolitical attacks, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into malicious operations, and the growth of connected energy technologies.

🔍 Overview

The event follows the release of ENISA’s Threat Landscape 2026, which analyzed 8,257 cyber incidents from 2025. The report found that attackers are increasingly incorporating AI into their operations while claims of intrusions related to operational technology (OT)—the systems used to control physical equipment and industrial processes—have increased.

🧩 How it works

The sector is observing how AI can be used as both a tool for attackers and a critical component of grid defense.

Entity AI and Cybersecurity Application
NPC Ukrenergo Uses AI to help cybersecurity teams react faster, identify gaps, support staff, and assist with reporting
Malicious Actors Incorporate AI into operations to shape geopolitical cyber activity and target OT systems
ENCS Identifies vulnerabilities in connected devices that use unauthenticated control protocols

⚙️ Key details

Recent real-world attacks provide a baseline for what grid cyber resilience requires in practice:

  • Poland (December 2025): A coordinated attack targeted wind and solar farms and a combined heat and power plant. Although electricity generation continued, attackers disrupted communications and gained access levels that could have enabled further disruption.
  • Ukraine: NPC Ukrenergo is sharing lessons on maintaining a grid under sustained attack, emphasizing the challenge of keeping specialist cybersecurity expertise when skilled teams are difficult to rebuild.
  • Connected Device Risks: ENCS researchers demonstrated that attackers can use compromised everyday devices, such as routers or cameras, to communicate with residential solar inverters or home batteries that lack command authentication.

💡 Why it matters

The expansion of high-power IoT devices creates a risk where manipulating thousands of units simultaneously could cause sudden changes in generation or demand, potentially leading to wider grid disturbances. Harm van den Brink, a security researcher at ENCS, noted that vulnerabilities in these devices have already been exploited and requires a shift toward independent security testing and manufacturer-led vulnerability management. Dimitra Liveri of ENISA stated that the challenge requires moving from protecting individual systems to optimizing the entire ecosystem for resilience.

#Cybersecurity #ArtificialIntelligence #EnergyGrid #GridResilience #EU

Source: E.DSO, EE-ISAC, ENCS and ENISA 9th Cybersecurity Forum – Press Release | E.DSO

item.title: Congress Debates Legislative Solutions for Rising AI Data Center Electricity Costs
item.description:
Congress Debates Legislative Solutions for Rising AI Data Center Electricity Costs

Congress is scrambling to address voter concerns over the impact of AI data centers on residential electricity rates as lawmakers debate new legislative measures. With the data center industry rapidly expanding, regional utilities are building tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in new infrastructure, raising questions about how much of these costs will be passed on to everyday utility customers.

⚖️ Legislative Initiatives

Several data center and AI-related bills are moving through Congress. The primary competing measures include:

Bill Name Sponsor / Promoter Key Provisions & Status
Ratepayer Protection Act Sponsored by Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted Would have state utilities consider holding “large-load” customers responsible for increased costs. Passed the House in September with strong bipartisan support; opposed by Senate Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer.
GRID Savings Act Authored by New Mexico Democrat Sen. Martin Heinrich; promoted by Sen. Chuck Schumer Aimed at protecting ratepayers; described by Schumer as having “more teeth” than the Ratepayer Protection Act because the Ratepayer Protection Act’s protections are voluntary.

⚙️ Rising Infrastructure and Utility Costs

The rapid growth of data centers has significantly impacted regional energy grids and wholesale electricity costs:

  • Overall Ratepayer Impact: PJM, a regional transmission organization serving 13 states and the District of Columbia (including Northern Virginia), has an Independent Market Monitor estimating that data centers have cost their 67 million ratepayers approximately $29 billion over roughly the past two years.
  • State-Level Costs: Maryland customers pay an estimated $168 to $216 more per year on electricity bills primarily due to the data center boom.
  • Infrastructure Demands: Utilities are constructing new power lines, substations, and other grid-connecting infrastructure. Connor Waldoch, co-founder and chief strategy officer at Grid Status, notes, “We’re talking tens to hundreds of millions of dollars [of infrastructure] that are being built by these local utilities.”
  • Cost Recovery: Jeremy L. Slayton, a spokesman for Dominion Energy, which serves Loudoun County, Virginia, stated, “We recover costs for distribution and transmission infrastructure from customers.”

🧩 Challenges in Determining Consumer Impact

Calculating the precise cost passed on to residential ratepayers is difficult due to several variables and a lack of transparency:

  • Local Variables: According to Lucy Qiu, a professor at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland, consumer impact depends on utilities’ power-purchasing contracts, retail rates, regulatory decisions, the scale of upgrades, and how utilities share accounting.
  • Lack of Transparency: Ari Peskoe, director of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative, states that a “single, clean number” for nationwide data center costs is impossible because much of the data regarding what data centers pay is hidden behind non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).
  • Prevalence of NDAs: A study by the University of Mary Washington found that NDAs had been signed in 80% of Virginia localities where there were existing, approved, or proposed data centers.

💡 Political Ramifications

The issue of data center growth and energy costs has also entered political campaigns. Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted is currently in a heated reelection campaign against Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his Senate seat in 2024. Brown has made Husted’s past support of data centers in Ohio a major campaign issue.

#AIdatacenters #EnergyPolicy #RatepayerProtection #GridInfrastructure

Source: Data centers
